progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m5-c13 (precipitation; which products are insoluble; BaSO₄ and AgCl white); chem-m5-c14 (Ksp; comparing Ksp only for the same formula type); chem-m5-c15 (the common ion effect); Year 11 (n = m/M, molar mass, percentage by mass); chem-m8-c01 (moles to concentration, c = n/V).
progression.startsWith: Choose a low-solubility product. The video opens: Last time, we counted chloride by measuring a volume of silver nitrate. This time, we'll weigh it. A wastewater sample looks perfectly clear.
progression.stopsAfter: stating what gravimetric analysis is and its three requirements; explaining the choice of Ba²⁺ for sulfate (and Ag⁺ for chloride) with Ksp; describing and justifying each method step, including constant mass; calculating the precipitate mass by difference, the analyte's moles, mass, percentage and concentration; predicting the direction of an error and explaining why repeats do not fix it. No hands-on procedure or risk table.
progression.nextLesson: carrying out a gravimetric analysis (route chem-m8-p02).

teaching.task: A clear wastewater sample turns cloudy white when barium ions are added. How does the mass of that dried solid tell you how much sulfate was in the water, and what has to go right for the number to be true?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a clear sample gives a white solid whose mass gives the sulfate; (2) the method works if almost all the ion is in the solid, its formula is known, and only it is weighed, clean and dry; (3) barium, not calcium, because barium sulfate's Ksp is far smaller (same formula type), so almost none stays dissolved, and excess barium lowers it more; sodium sulfate is soluble; silver for chloride; (4) excess reagent until no more forms; digestion grows bigger crystals that filter and trap less; (5) pre-weighed paper, rinse, wash away soluble ions that would add mass; (6) oven, desiccator so no water is taken up, tared watch glass, repeat to constant mass (drying has stopped removing water; dry impurities would also be constant, so washing still matters); (7, 8) mass by difference, n = m/M, 1 : 1, mass of sulfate, percentage; (9) concentration from a volume; (10) extra mass high, lost solid low; repeating the same faulty method keeps the error in the average.
teaching.conversationalApproach: last time chloride was counted by measuring a volume, and this time it is weighed: a clear wastewater sample gives a fine white solid with barium ions, and a chemist uses only its dried mass to find the sulfate, so the video asks how a precipitate reveals ion concentration. Gravimetric analysis means measuring by mass: turn the ion into a solid of known formula, collect all of it, dry it and weigh it, which works only if almost all the ion ends up in the solid, the solid is pure and its formula is known. Barium is chosen over calcium because both sulfates are one to one, so their Ksp values compare directly, and calcium sulfate's is about half a million times bigger. The method dissolves and acidifies the sample, adds excess barium chloride with a check drop, and digests the solid; it is filtered through a pre-weighed paper, rinsed and washed so no soluble ions dry onto it, then dried, cooled in a desiccator and reweighed to constant mass. The worked example finds the precipitate mass by difference, then moles, the one to one ratio, sulfate mass and the percentage, and then a concentration from a volume. Anything that adds mass makes the answer too high and anything that loses solid makes it too low. The memory aid is mass, moles, ratio, target, and too wet reads high, lost reads low. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Last time, we counted chloride by measuring a volume of silver nitrate. This time, we'll weigh it. A wastewater sample looks perfectly clear. Add barium ions, and a fine white solid appears. After it's filtered and dried, a chemist uses only its mass to work out how much sulfate was in the water. So how does a pinch of white powder tell you that?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) Creek water, 50.0 mL, excess AgNO₃, filter paper 0.812 g, paper and dry precipitate 0.955 g, M(AgCl) and M(Cl) given; chloride in g/L. Tests mass by difference, n = m/M, the 1 : 1 formula ratio, mass, and division by volume. Crossed mistake: not subtracting the paper (4.72 g/L). (A2) An unwashed BaSO₄ precipitate, repeated three times the same way and averaged: explain the effect on the sulfate percentage and assess whether repeating helps. Tests scene 5's cause and scene 10's last line. Crossed mistake: "averaging three trials cancels the error" (pack trap).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct investigations and/or process data involving:; gravimetric analysis; precipitation titrations" This video explains gravimetric analysis and processes its data. Precipitation titrations were chem-m8-c01; the hands-on gravimetric practical is chem-m8-p02; practice with both is chem-m8-g01. starts by choosing a low-solubility product, and stops at converting a dry precipitate's mass to the original ion's concentration (and percentage by mass). It teaches: gravimetric analysis (measuring by mass) and its three requirements (almost all the ion precipitates; known formula; only that solid is weighed, clean and dry); why Ba²⁺ for sulfate (BaSO₄ Ksp far smaller than CaSO₄'s, both 1 : 1 so Ksp compares directly; much less left dissolved (about 0.5 mg in 200 mL of pure water at 25 °C); excess Ba²⁺ lowers it further, the common ion effect) and why not Na⁺; Ag⁺ for chloride; the method: dissolve, acidify with dilute HCl so carbonate leaves as CO₂, add excess precipitating reagent and check for completeness, digest (small crystals dissolve and larger ones grow, which filter better and trap fewer ions), filter through pre-weighed filter paper, rinse and wash, dry in an oven, cool in a desiccator, weigh on a tared watch glass, repeat to constant mass (a dryness check; washing is the purity control); mass by difference; n = m/M; the formula ratio; analyte mass and percentage; concentration from a sample volume; error directions (extra mass reads high, lost solid reads low); repeating and averaging do not remove an error that is the same every time. Not taught: ignition in a crucible, co-precipitation mechanisms (author notes), the risk table (p02), the Mohr method (c01).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key: sulfate ions yellow-green; barium ions pale violet; calcium ions pale orange; chloride green; silver pale grey; precipitate white; spectator or impurity ions small grey dots; givens and units navy; the current answer bright; earlier lines dim. Board layout (constant): heading top-left; apparatus left third; inset or board right two thirds. Reuse: painted plates inspected 28 Oct by contact sheet (Assets). `m6-analytical-balance-v1.png` shows a small beaker of white powder on the pan, which contradicts the filter paper method, so a matching balance plate with a watch glass is commissioned; the existing one is used only in c01's handoff. No human figures.
